title: IP Allowlist / Network-Location Auth
subtitle: The 'credential' is where you are, not who you are — the same credential-free request succeeds on-net and fails off-net. Step through it and see why an IP address is not an identity.

steps.label: Access internal admin panel
steps.lede: The user opens an internal tool. Access will be decided entirely by the request's source IP — evaluated at the gateway, below the application.
steps.devtools: Open DevTools (F12) → Network. The striking thing here is what you will not see: any credential. The deciding factor — source IP — is not an HTTP artifact visible in the request.

steps.label: On-network GET /panel → 200
steps.lede: From an allowlisted source IP the request succeeds. Inspect it: no Authorization header, no auth cookie, no token. Nothing in the request says who is calling.

jwt.title: Gateway network context (NOT an HTTP artifact)
payload: The transport peer address the gateway actually evaluates (RFC 5737 doc range)
Peer is inside the range — request forwarded to the app

steps.devtools: In Request Headers confirm there is no Authorization, no auth Cookie, and no token. It succeeded solely because the source IP is allowlisted — a decision made at the gateway, invisible in the request contents.

steps.label: Off-network GET /panel → 403
steps.lede: The exact same request — byte-for-byte identical headers — now fails from an off-network IP. The only thing that changed is the network path, which you cannot see in the request.

jwt.title: Gateway network context
payload: Peer outside the range — rejected at the gateway

steps.devtools: Compare this row to the previous one: identical request, different status (403 vs 200). Ideally the service is not even discoverable off-net — a silent connection reset / net::ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT gives scanners no signal that it exists.

steps.label: Spoofed X-Forwarded-For → still 403
steps.lede: An attacker off-net adds X-Forwarded-For claiming an allowed IP. A correctly configured gateway ignores it and decides on the real transport peer — so the outcome is unchanged.

jwt.title: Gateway network context
payload: The REAL transport peer the gateway uses
Header ignored; real peer is outside the allowlist

steps.devtools: Add X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.5 and confirm the outcome does not change. A correct gateway decides on the transport peer (or a header set by infrastructure it owns), not a client-supplied one. If the outcome does change, the gateway is dangerously trusting a forgeable header.

steps.label: Layer real authentication on top
steps.lede: Because network location is not identity, the allowlist should be defense-in-depth under real authentication: allowlist as filter, IdP as authentication, network as a conditional-access signal.
steps.devtools: An authenticated variant would additionally carry a Cookie, Authorization, or token you would see in the Network tab. Everything behind a shared NAT/VPN/office egress looks identical, so a 200 here proves only network location, never who — treat the allowlist as one layer, not the whole story.
